Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

Because it is a flash fiction piece focused on a single, brief encounter, it appropriately unfolds primarily as a real-time scene featuring vivid sensory details (the wet rope, the rattling suitcase wheels, the smell of aftershave), action, and dialogue. However, the author seamlessly weaves brief moments of exposition and summary into the scene—such as the reference to the photos on Jonas's company website, Ilse's usual end-of-day routine, and the leftover potato soup on the stove. This provides just enough background information to establish the contrast between the mother's and son's lives and build subtle tension without disrupting the real-time pacing of their interaction.
